title: John 14:1–14
context: Let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me. He goes to prepare a place, and will come again. Thomas asks the way; Jesus is the way, the truth, and the life—no one comes to the Father except through Him. Philip asks to see the Father; to see Jesus is to see the Father. Those who believe will do His works, and whatever they ask in His name He will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: Arminian and Reformed writers of the past on the way to the Father and believing the Son, in their own words.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: Let not your heart be troubled: believe in God, believe also in me. I am the way, the truth, and the life; no man cometh unto the Father but by me. He that hath seen me hath seen the Father.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on John 14:1, 6, 9)

reformed.quote: He bids them believe in God, and believe in him: faith is the remedy for a troubled heart. No one comes to the Father but by me. He who has seen me has seen the Father: the whole fullness of the Godhead dwells in him.

verses.text: “Don’t let your heart be troubled. Believe in God. Believe also in me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Troubled hearts (13:38 still ringing) are met with a double believe. Faith in the Father and in the Son is the prescribed calm.

The command not to be troubled is not a scold; it is a path. They can believe; grace that has shown them the Son now steadies them in Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: faith is the remedy for a troubled heart. Believe in God; believe also in me—one trust with two named objects.

He does not offer a technique. He offers Himself as the object that stills.

verses.text: In my Father’s house are many homes. If it weren’t so, I would have told you. I am going to prepare a place for you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Many rooms: space in the Father’s house, not a shortage. He goes to prepare.

The house is the Father’s and the rooms are many. The going is for them; the question form presses them to trust His speech.
verses.reformedNotes:
Father’s house, many rooms, I go to prepare. The departure is hospitality, not abandonment.

He would not have told them a lie. The preparation is His work in leaving.

verses.text: If I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and will receive you to myself; that where I am, you may be there also.
verses.arminianNotes:
Go, come again, take you to myself—destination is a person: where I am.

The coming is as sure as the going. Being with Him is the point of the rooms.
verses.reformedNotes:
I will come again and take you to myself. Reunion is His action.

The prepared place is personal presence. Where I am is the definition of home.

verses.text: You know where I go, and you know the way.”
verses.arminianNotes:
He says they know the way. They will immediately prove they feel otherwise.

Knowing Jesus is knowing the way, even when they cannot yet diagram it.
verses.reformedNotes:
You know: already true in Him, not yet clear to them.

The way is not missing. It is standing in the room.

verses.text: Thomas said to him, “Lord, we don’t know where you are going. How can we know the way?”
verses.arminianNotes:
Thomas is honest: no where, so no how. The question is the disciple we need on the page.

Asking is not unbelief by itself. Jesus will answer with a person, not a map app.
verses.reformedNotes:
Where and way: Thomas wants coordinates.

He has heard 13:33–36 and still cannot plot it. The next verse will relocate way from route to Christ.

verses.text: Jesus said to him, “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father, except through me.
verses.arminianNotes:
I am—not I show—the way, truth, life. Exclusive: no one comes to the Father except through me. Wesley preached this without embarrassment.

Arminians hold the exclusivity and the wideness together: the only way is sincerely set before the world. Coming is a free act of faith in this Jesus; no rival path, no closed secret for a few who never hear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: no one comes but by me. Way, truth, life are not three products; they are one Son.

Access to the Father is located in Christ alone. The no one is as wide as humanity and as particular as this Mediator.
verses.keyContrast: Jesus alone is the way to the Father. Arminians typically emphasize that this unique way is sincerely offered to all who hear, to be taken by faith. Reformed commentators stress that coming through Him is the only access God has appointed, which He actually grants in the Son.

verses.text: If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on, you know him and have seen him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Knowing Jesus is knowing the Father. From now on: a turn in their knowledge, including seeing.

Not a ladder beyond Christ. The from now on is gospel—they may know, because they have seen Him.
verses.reformedNotes:
If you had known me: the Father is not behind Jesus but in Him.

From now on, you know. The seeing of v. 9 is already breaking in.

verses.text: Philip said to him, “Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Philip wants a theophany that would be enough. He has been looking at enough and calling it not enough.

We still ask for a showing beyond the Son. Jesus will not shame the hunger; He will relocate it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Show us the Father: the request sounds pious and misses the Incarnation in the room.

What Philip calls enough is already given in the face he sees.

verses.text: Jesus said to him, “Have I been with you such a long time, and do you not know me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father. How do you say, ‘Show us the Father’?
verses.arminianNotes:
So long, still not know. He who has seen me has seen the Father. Wesley and Calvin both camp here.

There is no Father-behind-the-curtain who contradicts the Son. Seeing Jesus is the showing Philip asked for.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: the whole fullness dwells in Him. Seen me / seen the Father is not metaphor-only.

The request “show the Father” after months with Jesus is the tragedy of unseeing sight.

verses.text: Don’t you believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me? The words that I tell you, I speak not from myself; but the Father who lives in me does his works.
verses.arminianNotes:
Mutual indwelling; words not on His own authority; the indwelling Father does the works. Speech and deed are the Father at work in the Son.

Do you not believe—belief is the missing piece, and it is called for. The works and words are sufficient ground.
verses.reformedNotes:
I in the Father, Father in me. Words and works are not freelance.

The Father dwelling does His works. Unbelief here is unbelief in the indwelling God.

verses.text: Believe me that I am in the Father, and the Father in me; or else believe me for the very works’ sake.
verses.arminianNotes:
Believe me, or else believe the works. Jesus offers two rungs to faith, both leading to the same union.

Even works-faith is invited if person-faith is slow. He meets them where they are without making signs the ceiling (cf. 4:48).
verses.reformedNotes:
Believe me / or else the works. He argues for the same truth from two witnesses.

The works themselves testify. He is not above giving a second handle to a slow faith.

verses.text: Most certainly I tell you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also; and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to my Father.
verses.arminianNotes:
Whoever believes will do His works, and greater, because He goes. Greater is harvest-wide (Acts), not a boast of better miracles than the incarnation.

Believing issues in works. The going to the Father (Spirit, 14:16) is why the greater can happen through ordinary believers.
verses.reformedNotes:
Truly, truly: believers as His work-doers, greater because of the going.

The departure is the engine. Pentecostal wideness, not a rivalry with the Son’s unique works.

verses.text: Whatever you will ask in my name, I will do it, that the Father may be glorified in the Son.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ask in my name, I will do, so that the Father is glorified in the Son. Prayer’s whatever is name-shaped and doxological.

They are invited to ask. The name binds request to His character; the doing is His, the glory the Father’s.
verses.reformedNotes:
I will do: the Son answers prayer in His name for the Father’s glory.

That the Father may be glorified in the Son. Prayer is not a vending machine; it is that glory.

verses.text: If you will ask anything in my name, I will do it.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ask me—the Son as hearer. Anything in my name, I will do it. The repetition is comfort, not a loophole.

They may ask Him. Faith prays; He acts. The name remains the fence and the access.
verses.reformedNotes:
If you ask me: Christ the addressee. I will do it: His agency.

The promise is as large as the name and as bound to it. Anything is not any whim; it is any request that can live in that name.
